level1.text: The energy levels of the hydrogen atom are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. What is the energy of the hydrogen atom when the electron is on level $n = 4$? Give the answer with its sign in electron volts.

The energy levels of the hydrogen atom are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. The electron of a hydrogen atom moves from level $n = 4$ to the ground state $n = 1$. What is the energy of the photon produced, in electron volts?

The hydrogen spectrum has a cyan line with a wavelength of $486\,\text{nm}$. What is the energy of a photon of this light? Give the answer in electron volts ($h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$).

The energy levels of the hydrogen atom are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. A hydrogen atom is in the excited state $n = 3$. How much energy is needed to free the electron from the atom from this state? Give the answer in electron volts.

The energy of a photon produced in a transition of a hydrogen atom is $1.89\,\text{eV}$. What is the frequency of the photon? Give the answer in terahertz ($1\,\text{THz} = 10^{12}\,\text{Hz}$; $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$).

The energy levels of the hydrogen atom are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. Consider four transitions $5 \to 4$, $3 \to 2$, $2 \to 1$ and $4 \to 1$, where the pair of numbers gives the initial level and the final level. Which transition emits the photon with the shortest wavelength?
level1.answer: $4 \to 1$, because the energy difference is the greatest, and a large photon energy means a short wavelength.

choices.text: $5 \to 4$, because the initial level is the highest, and the higher up the electron comes from, the greater the energy difference.
choices.feedback: The energy of the photon is the difference between the energies of the levels, not the height of the initial level. Up high the levels are close together near zero, so the difference $E_5 - E_4$ is only about $0.31\,\text{eV}$ and the wavelength is long, about $4000\,\text{nm}$.

choices.text: $3 \to 2$, because it produces visible light, and visible light has the shortest wavelength of all.
choices.feedback: Visible light does not have the shortest wavelength: the wavelength of ultraviolet radiation is shorter than that of visible light. The photon of the transition $3 \to 2$ has an energy of only about $1.89\,\text{eV}$ and a wavelength of $656\,\text{nm}$, whereas the transitions ending in the ground state are ultraviolet.

choices.text: $4 \to 1$, because the energy difference is the greatest, and a large photon energy means a short wavelength.
choices.feedback: Correct: the energy of the photon is the difference between the levels, and the wavelength is inversely proportional to the energy. The difference $E_4 - E_1 = 12.75\,\text{eV}$ is the greatest of the four, so the wavelength $97.3\,\text{nm}$ is the shortest.

choices.text: $2 \to 1$, because a transition ending in the ground state is always the biggest jump and gives the greatest energy.
choices.feedback: There are many transitions ending in the ground state, and the greatest energy difference comes from the initial level that is higher up. The difference $E_2 - E_1 = 10.2\,\text{eV}$ is smaller than $E_4 - E_1 = 12.75\,\text{eV}$, so $2 \to 1$ gives a longer wavelength.

level1.text: The transitions of the hydrogen atom that end in the ground state $n = 1$ form the Lyman series. The energy levels of the hydrogen atom are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. Calculate the longest wavelength of the series in nanometres ($h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$).

The energy levels of the hydrogen atom are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. A hydrogen atom on level $n = 2$ absorbs a photon and is excited to level $n = 4$. What is the energy of the absorbed photon in electron volts?

level2.text: The energy levels of the hydrogen atom are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. The electron of a hydrogen atom moves from level $n = 5$ to level $n = 2$. Calculate the wavelength of the light produced in nanometres ($h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$).

The energy levels of the hydrogen atom are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. The violet spectral line of hydrogen, with a wavelength of $410\,\text{nm}$, is produced in a transition that ends on level $n = 2$. From which level does the transition start? Give the number $n$ of the level as the answer.

The figure shows the energy-level diagram of an imaginary atom. The electron of the atom moves from level $E_3$ to level $E_2$. Calculate the wavelength of the photon produced in nanometres. Read the energies of the levels from the figure ($h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$).

An ultraviolet photon with a wavelength of $80.0\,\text{nm}$ hits a hydrogen atom in the ground state. The photon ionises the atom; the ionisation energy of hydrogen from the ground state is $13.6\,\text{eV}$. What is the kinetic energy of the freed electron in electron volts ($h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$)?

The table shows four lines of the Balmer series of hydrogen. Each line is produced in a transition from level $n$ to level $2$, and the uncertainty of the wavelengths is $\pm 0.5\,\text{nm}$. Denote the ionisation energy of hydrogen from the ground state by $E_\text{ion}$, so that $E_n = -\tfrac{E_\text{ion}}{n^2}$ and the frequency of the photon is $f = \tfrac{E_n - E_2}{h}$.

a) Calculate the frequencies of the lines, $f = \tfrac{c}{\lambda}$, and draw a graph of the points with $f$ as a function of $\tfrac{1}{n^2}$. Fit a straight line to the points.

b) Determine the slope of the fitted line and use it to deduce the ionisation energy $E_\text{ion}$ in electron volts. Explain why the points should lie on a straight line.

Enter the result of part b) in the box in electron volts ($h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$).

The figure shows the energy-level diagram of an imaginary atom. The atom is in the ground state $E_1$. Photons of five different wavelengths are sent to the atom, and the table gives their wavelengths. The atom absorbs a photon only if the energy of the photon corresponds to the difference between some level above the ground state and the ground state ($\pm 0.05\,\text{eV}$). How many of the photons in the table does the atom absorb?

Calculate the energies of the photons and compare them with the energy differences read from the diagram. Enter in the box the number of photons absorbed ($h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$).

level2.text:
A student solves a problem: “The electron of a hydrogen atom moves from level $n = 5$ to the ground state. On orbit $n = 5$ the electron is $5^2 = 25$ times farther from the nucleus than in the ground state, so the energy of the photon produced is $25$ times the ionisation energy of the ground state, $13.6\,\text{eV}$, that is $340\,\text{eV}$.” The energy levels of the hydrogen atom are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$.

a) Explain what is wrong in the student's reasoning.

b) Calculate the energy of the photon correctly.

Enter in the box the result of part b) in electron volts.

level3.text:
The energy levels of the hydrogen atom are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. In a discharge tube, electrons with a kinetic energy of $12.5\,\text{eV}$ collide with hydrogen atoms in the ground state. In a collision an atom can take from the electron only the share of energy that corresponds to the difference of some pair of its levels.

How many different wavelengths can the excited atoms emit when they return to the ground state, counting also the transitions that pass through intermediate levels? Count the different pairs of levels between which a transition is possible: each pair of levels gives one wavelength.

The helium ion $\text{He}^+$ has only one electron, like the hydrogen atom, but the nucleus has two protons. The energy levels of the ion are $E_n = -\tfrac{54.4\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. A line is observed in the spectrum of a star that is produced in the transition of the ion from level $n = 4$ to level $n = 3$. Calculate the wavelength of the line in nanometres ($h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$).

The energy levels of the hydrogen atom are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. In hot hydrogen gas one atom returns from level $n = 2$ to the ground state and emits a photon. The photon hits another hydrogen atom that is in the excited state $n = 2$. Is the energy of the photon enough to ionise this atom? If it is, what is the kinetic energy of the freed electron in electron volts?

Three emission lines were measured in the spectrum of a distant gas cloud. The cloud contains only hydrogen atoms, whose energy levels are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. All three lines are produced in transitions that end on the same level, but each line has a different initial level. The uncertainty of the wavelengths is $\pm 1\,\text{nm}$ ($h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$).

a) Calculate the energies of the photons of the lines and deduce on which level $n$ the transitions end, and explain why the other levels do not work. Also find the initial level of each line.

b) What is the minimum frequency a photon must have in order to ionise an atom from the level on which the transitions end? In which part of the spectrum is the corresponding threshold wavelength?

Enter in the box the frequency of part b) in terahertz.

data.caption: Emission lines of the cloud (example data)

level3.text:
Hydrogen gas in the ground state is illuminated with monochromatic ultraviolet light. Each atom absorbs one photon and is excited to the same higher level, from which it returns to the ground state emitting photons either directly or through intermediate levels. The energy levels of the hydrogen atom are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. The table shows the lines of the light emitted by the gas; the light of the source itself has been filtered out before the measurement. The uncertainty of the wavelengths is at most $1\,\text{nm}$ ($h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$).

a) Calculate the energies of the photons of the lines and identify the initial and final level of each line.

b) Deduce to which level the atoms were excited. Explain why the excitation level cannot be higher.

c) Calculate the wavelength of the ultraviolet source in nanometres.

Enter in the box the result of part c).
